clinicalPearls: A gonadotropin-independent cause of precocious puberty affecting boys, with early virilisation (penile and pubic hair growth, accelerated linear growth) usually apparent in the first few years of life

Testicular enlargement is typically modest and often disproportionately small for the degree of virilisation, because Leydig cells are activated autonomously without the FSH-driven seminiferous tubule growth of true central puberty

Serum testosterone is elevated to pubertal levels while basal and GnRH-stimulated luteinising hormone and follicle-stimulating hormone are suppressed, confirming that the process is independent of the hypothalamic-pituitary axis

Inheritance is autosomal dominant with transmission through affected males or unaffected female carriers; girls carrying the same mutation are clinically unaffected because ovarian steroidogenesis requires both LH and FSH signalling
Bone age is markedly advanced, threatening premature epiphyseal fusion and compromised adult height if untreated

Medical management is directed at blocking androgen synthesis and action (an aromatase inhibitor to limit oestrogen-driven bone maturation combined with an androgen-receptor antagonist), rather than the GnRH analogues used for central precocious puberty

Long-standing peripheral sex-steroid exposure can secondarily activate the hypothalamic-pituitary-gonadal axis, converting the picture into mixed or central precocious puberty that then also responds to GnRH analogue therapy
reference.pathophysiology: Familial male-limited precocious puberty is caused by a germline activating (gain-of-function) mutation of the luteinising hormone/choriogonadotropin receptor (LHCGR) expressed on testicular Leydig cells. The mutant receptor signals constitutively through the cAMP pathway in the absence of ligand, driving autonomous testosterone production and Leydig cell activity that are entirely independent of pituitary gonadotropins. Because ovarian oestrogen synthesis requires cooperative FSH and LH action, isolated LH-receptor activation does not cause precocity in females, explaining the male-limited phenotype. The resulting early androgen exposure produces virilisation and rapid skeletal maturation, and sustained peripheral sex steroids may eventually prime the hypothalamus, superimposing true central precocious puberty.
additionalDifferentials: Central (gonadotropin-dependent) precocious puberty from hypothalamic-pituitary activation
Congenital adrenal hyperplasia or a virilising adrenal tumour
Leydig cell tumour of the testis producing androgens
Human chorionic gonadotropin-secreting tumour (e.g. hepatoblastoma, germ cell tumour) stimulating the LH receptor
McCune-Albright syndrome with autonomous gonadal activation
additionalInvestigations: Serum testosterone (elevated) with basal LH and FSH (suppressed)
GnRH (LHRH) stimulation test showing a prepubertal, suppressed gonadotropin response
Bone-age radiograph of the left hand and wrist to quantify skeletal advancement
Adrenal androgen profile (17-hydroxyprogesterone, DHEAS, androstenedione) to exclude adrenal causes
Beta-hCG measurement to exclude an hCG-secreting tumour
Molecular genetic testing for an activating LHCGR mutation and family screening
redFlags: Rapidly advancing bone age threatening early epiphyseal closure and short adult stature
Signs suggesting an alternative or additional pathology, such as a palpable testicular or abdominal mass
Very high testosterone with virilisation disproportionate to a familial pattern, prompting a tumour search
Emergence of significant testicular enlargement suggesting secondary central puberty superimposed on the primary disorder
reference.prognosis: With early recognition and combined androgen-blocking therapy, virilisation is controlled and skeletal maturation slowed, preserving adult height potential; untreated disease leads to accelerated bone maturation, premature fusion, and compromised final height, though fertility in adulthood is often preserved.
pitfalls: Reaching for GnRH analogues first, which are ineffective in the gonadotropin-independent phase and only help once secondary central puberty develops
Misreading small testes with marked virilisation as evidence against precocious puberty
Overlooking the diagnosis in a boy without a clear family history, as de novo mutations occur
Failing to reassess for superimposed central precocious puberty during follow-up
Attributing all early virilisation to adrenal causes without a GnRH stimulation test
management: Block peripheral androgen action and synthesis using an androgen-receptor antagonist (such as bicalutamide or spironolactone) combined with an aromatase inhibitor to curb oestrogen-driven skeletal maturation
Consider a steroidogenesis inhibitor such as ketoconazole as an adjunct to suppress autonomous testosterone production
Monitor growth velocity, bone age and predicted adult height to guide therapy and preserve height potential
Add a GnRH analogue if sustained androgen exposure superimposes secondary central precocious puberty
Provide psychological and developmental support for the child and family addressing early virilisation
Undertake molecular LHCGR testing and genetic counselling, noting female carriers are clinically unaffected but transmit the trait
Maintain paediatric endocrinology follow-up through puberty with attention to later fertility
